public_rationale: On July 20, 2023, OpenAI acknowledged that some tasks could worsen while saying most metrics had improved [e6]. An independent study, revised October 31, 2023, found both improvements and regressions between March and June 2023 model versions [e7]. On November 6, 2023, OpenAI reported improved instruction and format following [e8]. These sources establish the narrower admission about possible task regressions, but do not provide a consistent comparison of broad capability gains per unit of time across November 30, 2022–March 18, 2024 [e6, e7, e8]. They therefore settle neither a slowdown nor an equal or faster pace of improvement [e6, e7, e8].
limitations: The evidence lacks a consistent broad capability time series covering the full comparison period [e6, e7, e8].
The study compares March and June 2023 snapshots; it does not establish the trend through March 18, 2024 [e7].
The company reports do not quantify the overall rate of capability improvement [e6, e8].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The pace of capability improvement in OpenAI's models has slowed.

statement.excerpt: Murati and Altman's futures depend heavily on keeping the world believing that development and improvement of their models' capabilities will continue a rapacious pace of progress that has unquestionably slowed, with OpenAI admitting that GPT-4 may be worse on some tasks.

from_speaker: development and improvement of their models' capabilities
a rapacious pace of progress that has unquestionably slowed
OpenAI admitting that GPT-4 may be worse on some tasks
our_interpretation: The graded proposition concerns the pace of OpenAI capability improvement, not the separate assertion about executives' futures.
The ordinary reading requires smaller broad capability gains per unit of time compared with an earlier period. Continued improvement can coexist with slowing progress.
The comparison window is the ChatGPT era, November 30, 2022 through March 18, 2024. This supplies a plausible baseline from context, but the speaker did not specify one.
Task-specific regressions establish the narrower admission, not necessarily a slowdown in overall capability improvement.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable evaluations across successive OpenAI releases show a materially slower rate of broad capability improvement in the later part of the target period than in the earlier part.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evaluations across successive releases show broad capability gains continuing at an equal or faster rate over the same comparison periods.

evidence.locator: July 20, 2023 update, paragraph discussing evaluation metrics
evidence.explanation: This verifies that OpenAI acknowledged possible regressions on some tasks. The same sentence says most metrics improved, and neither statement measures whether the overall pace had slowed.

evidence.publisher: arXiv; Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou
evidence.explanation: The study documents regressions alongside improvements on other tasks. It compares two snapshots of existing services, rather than estimating the broad rate of capability improvement through March 2024.

OpenAI reported further capabilities and better format following later in 2023. This qualifies an impression of uniformly deteriorating models, but improvement by itself does not disprove slowing improvement.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Comparable evaluations of successive OpenAI models from November 30, 2022 through March 18, 2024, using consistent tasks, prompting and scoring, with a justified baseline and accounting for benchmark ceilings and new modalities, showing whether broad capability gains per unit of time slowed, stayed equal or accelerated.
